gist: AppLovin's CEO (Adam) and CTO (Gio) explain how a ~100-person engineering team rebuilt the ad ranking engine from tree-based models to embedding-plus-deep-neural-network 'Axon 2', taking the company from a ~$5.5B valuation and a 92% post-IPO drawdown to a ~$100B market cap on an EBITDA run rate they describe as over $7B. They lay out the arithmetic of getting to a trillion dollars (~$30B+ annual cash flow), why gaming UA dollars alone can't fund it, why chatbot ads are a poor fit for their top-of-funnel product while CTV and the open web are the real expansion targets, and why headcount discipline plus 'taste' is the operating model they think most companies cannot copy.

insights.claim: AppLovin's pre-2023 ad engine (Axon 1) was a tree-based model with hundreds of thousands of if-else branches clustering user-item pairs, which could not capture dynamic relationships that shift with time, weather, promotions and holidays.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: The step-change in AppLovin's revenue is architectural, not cyclical — competitors still running tree-based ranking carry a structural accuracy deficit that is expensive to close.
insights.quote: these treebased models are not able to accurately model this dynamic and relationship between user and items

insights.claim: Axon 2 replaced clustering with learnable embedding tables that encode user IDs and item IDs into semantically meaningful vectors passed through a deep neural network, which the CTO says extrapolates better to unseen user-item pairs.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: The same architecture pattern that powers LLMs is now the ad-ranking standard; ad-tech firms without embedding-based stacks are a generation behind.
insights.quote: we use the learnable embedding tables to encode those ID like item ID user ID that otherwise would make no no meaning

insights.claim: The neural-network engine is cheaper to run than the tree-based predecessor because it reduces to general matrix multiplication, which GPUs are highly optimized for, whereas selection-tree structures are hard to optimize on GPU hardware.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: Better accuracy arrived with lower unit inference cost — a rare margin-and-revenue double, which helps explain AppLovin's margin profile rather than treating it as pricing power.
insights.quote: the new generation model is very very powerful and efficient with a with a modern GPU architecture

insights.claim: Prediction accuracy is the direct causal driver of AppLovin's revenue: better predictions produce better advertiser returns, which pulls in more spend without a salesforce.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: Model-quality releases are the leading indicator to track for AppLovin revenue, not headcount, ad inventory or macro ad budgets.
insights.quote: Once we able to make prediction more accurate, advertisers see better returns and our business grow.

insights.claim: AppLovin is currently training a new generation of model beyond Axon 2, with the same engineering headcount, because AI tooling has raised per-engineer output.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: A next-gen model is in flight — a potential repeat of the Axon 2 revaluation catalyst, and a reason not to underwrite AppLovin purely off current model performance.
insights.quote: Now with the the assistance of AI, the team was able to tackle and work on a new generation of model that would be even more powerful.

insights.claim: AppLovin's engineering culture assumes the core engine will be thrown away and rearchitected every couple of years or faster, treating tech debt tolerance as an existential risk rather than a tradeoff.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Judge ad-tech and algorithmic platforms on willingness to cannibalize their own stack; the ones defending legacy systems are the short candidates.
insights.quote: technology moves really fast and you got to be humble about what you have and know that if technology goes faster than what you've developed, you got to throw away what you have and rearchitect, rebuild it

insights.claim: AppLovin's in-game ads run roughly 60 seconds and are playable mini-games rather than static banners, so each impression generates interaction data closer to a TV spot with telemetry than to a display ad.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: The data advantage is a function of ad format, not just scale — a competitor buying similar reach on 3-second social formats cannot replicate the training signal.
insights.quote: the ads inside games are much more similar to what television is but specifically for games you have somewhere around 60 seconds that people sit on an ad

insights.claim: A user seeing 10 AppLovin ads a day generates about 10 minutes of engagement, versus roughly 40 minutes a day a user spends on a highly successful social property — making the ad network itself a meaningful engagement surface.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Benchmark AppLovin's data collection against social platforms' total session time, not against display ad networks — the gap is far smaller than reach comparisons suggest.
insights.quote: If a user sees 10 ads on our platform a day that's 10 minutes of engagement with the website effectively that's like a miniame serving website.

insights.claim: AppLovin optimizes to post-install revenue, not installs — advertisers feed back downstream purchase and ad-revenue data so the model can close the loop from impression to monetized user.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: The moat is closed-loop attribution data supplied by advertisers; any privacy or data-sharing regime change that breaks that loop is the key risk to model quality.
insights.quote: But just a download for us means nothing. We're trying to deliver to the advertiser engagement and revenue.

insights.claim: The heavy mobile casual gamer is a 30-to-50-year-old head of household skewing slightly female — not the teenage gamer stereotype — which is why gaming-sourced behavioral data transfers to e-commerce buying.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: The bear case that 'they only have gaming data' misreads the audience; the panel is mainstream household purchasers, which supports the e-commerce expansion thesis.
insights.quote: the people who were playing mobile casual games turn out to be a lot of heads of households. It skews slightly female, but it is this sort of 30 to 50 year old age group that's the heavy mobile casual gamer

insights.claim: AppLovin explicitly copied Facebook's playbook of pixeling advertiser websites to learn user behavior beyond its own property, rejecting the analyst framing that its data is verticalized to gaming.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Management directly rebuts the most common short thesis; the testable question is pixel coverage growth on non-gaming advertiser properties.
insights.quote: we took the same approach started pixeling websites started getting data understood the user more than just their game behavior

insights.claim: The model architecture was designed to be vertical-agnostic from the start, so extending from gaming into e-commerce required new pipelines and product flows but not a new core model.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: Marginal cost of entering each new advertiser vertical is plumbing, not R&D — supporting faster-than-expected vertical rollouts.
insights.quote: we felt that the the core the core technology should be general enough to support different verticals

insights.claim: AppLovin is running at over a $7 billion EBITDA run rate and converts roughly 75% of each EBITDA dollar to cash after stock-based compensation.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: A concrete, management-stated cash conversion ratio to anchor any DCF — and one that already nets out SBC, unlike most adjusted-EBITDA disclosures.
insights.quote: we probably on an EBITD do basis, I think we're over a 7 billion run rate and we generate somewhere around 75% cash off the Ebbit dollar

insights.claim: AppLovin's EBITDA run rate is roughly 20x what it was three years ago, per the CEO's own comparison.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Quantifies the Axon 2 inflection; useful for stress-testing how much of the current multiple is a durable step-change versus a one-time catch-up.
insights.quote: If you took us 3 years ago that number was much much smaller. It was probably 120th of where we've gotten to in 3 years.

insights.claim: The CEO frames a trillion-dollar valuation as requiring $30 billion or more of annual cash flow, an explicit internal target roughly 5-6x current cash generation.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Gives investors management's own valuation arithmetic — back out the required revenue to hit $30B FCF and test whether the addressable ad pool supports it.
insights.quote: To take it from this scale up and be worth a trillion. We've got to believe that we can get to 30 billion plus of cash flow a year.

insights.claim: Mobile gaming user-acquisition dollars are too small a pool to support a trillion-dollar valuation, which is the stated reason AppLovin moved into consumer/e-commerce advertising.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Management concedes the core market is capped; the entire long-term bull case rests on non-gaming verticals executing, making e-commerce disclosure the number that matters.
insights.quote: the mobile gaming category is not big enough in terms of user acquisition dollars to support the type of cash flow we need to be valued at a trillion dollars

insights.claim: Even consumer/e-commerce expansion is insufficient to reach a trillion dollars on a five-year-plus horizon, so AppLovin is explicitly looking for additional adjacent categories beyond its current roadmap.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Expect further category entries or capability builds to be announced; the CEO is pre-signaling that the current product set is not the terminal business.

insights.claim: AppLovin has no intention of becoming a hyperscaler and runs with minimal capex, positioning it as an asset-light compounder rather than an AI infrastructure spender.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Differentiates AppLovin from AI-capex-heavy names: FCF is not going to be consumed by datacenter buildout, which supports continued buybacks.
insights.quote: we don't have much capbacks

insights.claim: AppLovin's headcount is roughly 400 people, down from about 600 two-to-three years ago, with engineering at about 100 people — essentially flat while the business scaled roughly 20x in EBITDA.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Revenue per employee is the standout metric here; it also means incremental revenue drops through at extreme margins, and that key-person risk is concentrated.

insights.claim: AppLovin fell 92% in its first 18 months as a public company after IPO'ing at a $30 billion market cap, and recovered to roughly $100 billion only after shipping Axon 2.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: A live case study that a single technology release, not cost cuts or narrative, drove a 90%+ drawdown recovery — the template for underwriting busted algorithmic platforms.
insights.quote: We dropped 92% in the first 18 months of being public. That dream seemed very, very far away, but post Axon 2, we recovered and now we're hundred billion dollar company.

insights.claim: Companies that grant stock-based compensation as a fixed percentage of equity get trapped in a dilution death spiral after a 90% drawdown; AppLovin avoided it by budgeting SBC in fixed dollar terms with a deliberately small headcount.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: A concrete screen for busted growth names: check whether SBC is dollar-denominated or share-denominated before betting on a recovery.
insights.quote: If the stock goes down 90%, are you going to issue 30% dilution every year? You'd never recover from that.

insights.claim: AppLovin stopped doing investor relations entirely for over a year at the bottom, on the view that a cheap valuation with no articulable growth story is unsellable to investors.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Contrarian to standard IR advice — management effort at a bottom is better spent on the product than the narrative, and an IR blackout is not necessarily a red flag.
insights.quote: we're rebuilding our technology stock is dirt cheap, but nobody buys something that's dirt cheap. They want to see a vision.

insights.claim: The CEO's stated view is that cheapness alone never attracts buyers because assets trade where they deserve to trade; only expected growth re-rates a stock.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to pure value screens — pairs with the argument that a catalyst, not a multiple, is what closes a discount.
insights.quote: they very rarely tend to buy something where they think it's just cheap because things trade wherever they deserve to trade

insights.claim: During the drawdown AppLovin deployed every dollar of cash flow and more into buying back its own shares, treating itself as its best available investment because internal conviction in the model rebuild exceeded market expectations.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Levered buybacks at the bottom were the mechanical amplifier on the recovery; look for the same setup (cash-generative, algorithmic, undervalued, low dilution) elsewhere.
insights.quote: We're just going to buy our own shares. We're going to become our best investor.

insights.claim: Enterprise SaaS companies in deep drawdowns will struggle to recover because their growth requires hiring go-to-market people rather than shipping algorithms, so re-accelerating revenue increases burn while the stock is low.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: A structural distinction between algorithmic and salesforce-driven businesses — argues against blanket 'beaten-down SaaS will mean-revert' trades.
insights.quote: especially when you talk about enterprise SAS, very robust platforms, but they're not algorithmic. So how do you actually accelerate revenue without go to market teams?

insights.claim: The CEO predicts that beaten-down public companies with low cash-flow multiples will increasingly be taken private by private equity, because the only fix — mass layoffs, cash extraction and leverage — fits the PE model and no longer fits public markets.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Supports a take-private/event-driven screen on low-multiple, high-cash-flow public software rather than a fundamental recovery thesis.
insights.quote: they start getting accumulated by private equity or or effectively plucked off the public markets taken private because the only way to recover it is a complete restructure

insights.claim: AppLovin's engineering headcount has been flat at roughly 100 people for three years while business scale and problem complexity grew sharply, which the CTO attributes to AI advancement arriving in sync with the company's growth curve.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: A rare quantified example of AI decoupling revenue growth from headcount growth — the clearest operating-leverage evidence for the AI-productivity thesis.
insights.quote: our team was elevated by AI. So we were able to manage the same size of the team while we're solving more challenging problems.

insights.claim: The CTO's framing is that engineers should sit on top of AI rather than beside it, continuously moving up to whatever AI is still bad at — currently long-horizon planning, while AI already handles question-answering, code writing and research.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: A usable job-design heuristic for evaluating whether a company's workforce will compound with AI or be displaced by it.
insights.quote: I don't want our engineer to see it next to AI. I want our engineer to see it on top of AI.

insights.claim: AppLovin distinguishes prototype systems (dashboards, one-off presentations, where AI can write anything) from core infrastructure that must stay clean, and holds the human engineer accountable for every decision the AI made on their behalf.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: A governance model for AI-generated code that avoids the codebase-rot risk other companies are accumulating — a differentiator worth asking about in any software diligence.
insights.quote: You can use AI however you want. But in the end of the day, you as a human is is held accountable for every decision that you your AI made for you.

insights.claim: The CTO says engineers still need to learn to code today because AI regularly makes bad coding decisions that a non-coder cannot judge or correct — and notes AppLovin's codebase remains clean while other companies are hitting that problem.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: Tempers the 'no one needs to code' narrative; also implies a coming quality divergence between firms with and without coding-literate reviewers.
insights.quote: If our engineers are not capable for coding themselves they will not be able to judge and correct that mistake.

insights.claim: AppLovin runs with almost no product management — a sub-handful of PMs against roughly 100 engineers — and its e-commerce data engine was designed by engineers on a napkin at breakfast without any business-team spec.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: The org design is a real cost and speed advantage, but also means the growth engine depends on a handful of business-literate engineers — concentrated key-person risk.
insights.quote: one of the cultural philosophies we had is almost no product management and have engineers that are competent enough about business problems to just write their own architecture

insights.claim: New hires and interns at AppLovin push code to production within their first week with no training program, on the CEO's theory that the fast real-world feedback loop is both a learning accelerant and a retention tool for high-IQ graduates who would otherwise not choose advertising.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Explains how a non-glamorous ad company competes for AI talent against frontier labs without paying frontier-lab compensation.
insights.quote: whether Gio is an intern or a full-time employee just started maybe even right out of school, um they can push code within the first week of being here

insights.claim: The CEO argues most incumbent organizations cannot become AI-native because you would effectively have to replace nearly everyone and rebuild the culture, and existing staff may resist AI adoption to justify their own jobs.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Bearish for enterprise AI transformation stories at legacy firms; the productivity gains may accrue mostly to companies already built lean.
insights.quote: technically you almost have to to replace near everyone and rebuild the culture up to be able to to deal with the world as it is today but that's not really possible for most companies

insights.claim: Handing teams an AI budget without structure produces duplicated slop — business people and engineers both building dashboards while the company pays Anthropic and OpenAI for the same work twice.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: A caution on reading enterprise LLM spend as a proxy for productivity — seat and token growth can reflect waste rather than output.
insights.quote: Everyone's paying anthropic and open AI for the same stuff. Like it's like what what are we doing here?

insights.claim: The CTO argues AI-driven output gains are being offset at many companies because cheaper building leads to more bad decisions and wasteful ideas, so AI does not change which problem needs solving.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: Explains why measured enterprise AI ROI keeps disappointing despite real per-task productivity gains — selection quality, not throughput, is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: AI really helps helps us to solve the problem but actually doesn't change the problem we have to solve

insights.claim: On the business side AppLovin's plan is to automate most repeatable processes within a couple of years and redeploy people into QBRs and relationship work, on the view that its AI can understand its own business but not each advertiser's business.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Sets expectation that AppLovin's revenue scaling will not require go-to-market headcount growth — protecting margins as the advertiser base widens.

insights.claim: In an ad system where targeting and bidding are fully automated, ad creative is the last variable an advertiser controls that can generate outperformance.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Points to durable demand for creative tooling and studios even as media buying commoditizes — the value migrates to whoever makes the asset.
insights.quote: this is one of those variables that can create alpha in an advertising system. The advertisers that invest in creative and are good at it ... can create lifts in an advertising system where everything else is automated.

insights.claim: There is no formula for a winning ad; the CEO, with 21 years in advertising, says advertisers should produce roughly 30 conceptually differentiated ads a week and expect about one to be interesting.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Quantifies the shots-on-goal required, which is the volume argument behind generative creative tooling demand.
insights.quote: If you create 30 ads a week, probably one of those might be interesting.

insights.claim: UGC-style social creative underperforms on AppLovin because social ads are built to hook in 3 seconds while AppLovin gives an advertiser 60 seconds with a differently-wired, older user — so advertisers who port social creative directly leave returns on the table.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Cuts against the consensus that UGC creative is universally superior; early advertisers who build format-native creative on AppLovin capture measurable excess return.
insights.quote: a social ad will say you got 3 seconds to capture attention that's it

insights.claim: Generative AI cannot yet produce a 30-to-60-second brand-safe video ad without errors, so today's AI impact on advertising is humans making ads faster and cheaper, not a flood of machine-generated campaigns.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Deflates near-term expectations for fully automated ad generation startups while confirming rising ad-content volume — tailwind for assistive tools, not autonomous ones.
insights.quote: The challenge is to get them to put together a 30 to 60sec video advertisement for a brand that doesn't mess anything up

insights.claim: AppLovin distinguishes two AI creative product models — fully automatic generation versus human-collaborative tools — and says only the collaborative type has achieved wide adoption, while AppLovin must build the fully automatic version because it serves all advertisers, not one.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: AppLovin is actively building fully automated creative generation — a potential new product line and a competitive threat to assistive creative vendors.
insights.quote: we're not serving one single advertiser. We're serving all the advertisers. We have to create a tool that can fully automate everything.

insights.claim: AppLovin has looked at influencer-creative AI tools such as Higgsfield and concluded they solve the wrong problem, because short social clips do not meet the brand-trust bar of a large advertiser — so AppLovin builds rather than buys.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Lowers the probability of AppLovin M&A in generative creative and signals that current AI creative startups are not positioned for enterprise brand demand.
insights.quote: if you get a brand as big as a Wayfair and you hand them something out of the box that looks not ideal for their brand, they lose trust in you as a platform

insights.claim: Chatbot advertising will most likely resemble bottom-of-funnel search advertising because roughly 99% of consumer AI usage is search-like — which makes it a poor fit for AppLovin's top-of-funnel discovery product.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: The LLM ad opportunity accrues to search-native players, not discovery networks — useful for handicapping who captures chatbot ad dollars.
insights.quote: If 99% of the use case is search, then the ads in chat bots are probably going to look and feel a lot like search.

insights.claim: AppLovin's expansion R&D is aimed at connected TV and video placements in the open web, chosen specifically because those are discovery environments where the user does not know what they want.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Names the next two expansion vectors before they are products — an early read on where AppLovin's incremental TAM will be claimed, and a competitive signal for CTV incumbents.
insights.quote: an example of that that we've been working on and and still doing some research and development on to see if we can extend our platform to is connected TV, television

insights.claim: Mobile is a duopoly where any consumer business must sit on Apple or Google, but connected TV and the open web are structurally fragmented with no dominant operating system — so AppLovin's next markets will look more open than its current one.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Expansion into fragmented environments reduces AppLovin's platform-dependency risk on Apple and Google, a persistent overhang on the current business.
insights.quote: you're just in such a duopoly state in mobile

insights.claim: The CEO does not expect frontier labs to become operating systems, so even LLM-based advertising would be fragmented across many destinations rather than gatekept by one platform.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Argues against the thesis that a single AI lab captures an app-store-like distribution chokepoint — relevant to valuing platform-tax assumptions at the labs.
insights.quote: would one of these frontier labs become an operating system? It doesn't look like they're going that way.

insights.claim: The CEO rejects the view that chatbots completing transactions will kill ad-driven e-commerce, arguing people genuinely enjoy shopping, browsing products and receiving packages.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: A direct pushback on the agentic-commerce bear case for retail media and e-commerce ad networks.
insights.quote: people actually like to shop and people want to look at different products and people want to click buttons on a shopping site and people want to hit buy

insights.claim: AppLovin entered the consumer e-commerce vertical roughly 18 months ago and considers the market so early that it must still educate advertisers and agencies on what works — which is precisely why early advertisers can capture excess returns.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Suggests e-commerce revenue is still in the education phase, implying the ramp is not yet reflecting mature spend levels.
insights.quote: We got into this this consumer vertical and more specifically e-commerce 18 months ago roughly.

insights.claim: The CTO attributes Axon's success mainly to what the team decided not to build rather than what it built, arguing small teams that try to replicate every component of a giant's system are guaranteed to lose.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: A diligence question for any challenger: what did they deliberately not build? Breadth-matching against incumbents is the failure mode to screen out.
insights.quote: I would attribute the success of of Axon, you know, largely to what we decide not to do, not actually what we did.

insights.claim: Both executives argue the main differentiator in the AI era is taste — knowing what to build and what not to build — not the ability to build, and that taste includes engineering taste, not just aesthetics.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: If building is commoditized, the moat metric shifts from engineering headcount to decision quality — which is invisible in financial screens and only shows up in shipped roadmaps.
insights.quote: It's the taste. It's a taste to know what to build and what not to build.

insights.claim: Because AI lets everyone produce competent output, companies must deliberately create variance to generate alpha — the same logic applies to code and to ad creative, where uniform AI output would stop working on users.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: A non-obvious cross-domain claim: AI homogenization degrades ad response rates industry-wide, which raises the value of differentiated creative over time.
insights.quote: if the AI starts writing all the ad creative then all of it's going to eventually look the same and the user won't respond to the ad

insights.claim: The CTO screens hires for intelligence plus low ego, arguing low ego is the overlooked trait because it produces self-questioning — and that the danger for proven high performers is that nobody around them challenges them anymore.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: A hiring and management heuristic, and a warning sign to watch in successful founder-led companies where the leadership has stopped being questioned.
insights.quote: When a person has low ego, he tend to listen. He tends to empower his team, tends to help others and more importantly they they take feedbacks and then they proactively question themselves

insights.claim: The CTO uses VS Code with Claude for coding and has switched from Gemini to ChatGPT for text work in the past year, noting he switched the other direction a year earlier — evidence that even sophisticated technical buyers churn between frontier models annually.
insights.speaker: Gio, AppLovin CTO
insights.so_what: Model switching costs at the individual power-user level appear near zero, undermining assumptions of durable lock-in for any single frontier lab.
insights.quote: I used to be a Gemini person but recently I switched to Chachib

insights.claim: The CEO reframes advertising as economically generative — creating transactions that would not otherwise occur — and applies the same marketing logic to AI, arguing public hostility to AI persists because people only see it as a search engine and hear job-loss messaging.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Implies AI adoption is a marketing/narrative problem as much as a capability problem — relevant to timing consumer AI monetization.
insights.quote: until people start understanding what the average person can have as positive use cases that are incremental to search, they're not going to be proponents of AI

insights.claim: AppLovin raised its seed round at a $4 million valuation and was told large companies would put it out of business — the CEO frames perpetual disadvantage as the company's operating default rather than a phase it escaped.
insights.speaker: Adam, AppLovin CEO
insights.so_what: Context for management's risk appetite: the same posture that produced the buyback-at-the-bottom decision is likely to drive aggressive expansion bets.
insights.quote: we were told when we were went out first looking for seed funding a $4 million valuation, big companies are going to put us out of business
